value.overview: The White-collared Swift (Streptoprocne zonaris) is a large, fast-flying swift of the American tropics. It is usually seen in noisy flocks, often high above forests, mountains, valleys, and open country while pursuing flying insects. Its mostly black plumage, bold white collar, long pointed wings, and deeply notched tail make it distinctive. In Costa Rica, it is a widespread native species recorded from both lowlands and montane areas.
value.classification: The White-collared Swift belongs to the swift family Apodidae and the subfamily Cypseloidinae. It is one of the largest swifts in the Americas.
value.identification: Adults are about 22 centimeters long and appear predominantly black, with long, narrow, pointed wings and a fairly long, forked or deeply notched tail. A broad, conspicuous white collar surrounds the back and sides of the neck and extends across the upper breast. The collar may look less sharply defined in immature birds. In flight, its large size, powerful wingbeats, gliding periods, and contrasting collar separate it from most other Costa Rican swifts.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from Mexico through Central America and the Caribbean to much of South America. In Costa Rica it is a native, regularly occurring species, with records from many regions including the central highlands, northern slopes, Caribbean lowlands, and Pacific areas. It uses a broad range of landscapes, including humid forest, cloud forest, wooded valleys, foothills, agricultural country, and open areas. It often forages over mountains, ridges, forest edges, rivers, and waterfalls, sometimes traveling far from nesting sites.
value.migrationStatus: The White-collared Swift is generally considered resident in Costa Rica rather than a long-distance migrant. Numbers and locations may vary locally with weather, insects, and elevation, and flocks can make broad daily movements while feeding.
value.breeding: White-collared Swifts nest colonially on steep rock faces, in caves, and behind or near waterfalls, where damp sheltered surfaces provide suitable attachment sites. The nest is a small cup made from mosses, plant fibers, and other material secured with mud or saliva. Breeding biology is incompletely documented across its range, but the species usually lays a small clutch and both adults are believed to share incubation and care of the young. In Costa Rica, suitable cliffs, caves, and waterfall sites are important breeding habitat.
value.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on flying insects, including beetles, ants, bees, wasps, termites, flies, and other small aerial arthropods. White-collared Swifts usually forage in open airspace, often high above the ground, and may gather in large mixed or single-species flocks where insect concentrations are strong. They capture prey during sustained, highly maneuverable flight and may exploit updrafts along mountain slopes, ridges, and valleys.
value.behavior: This is a highly aerial species that spends much of its life in flight. Flocks are often conspicuous because of their size, rapid wingbeats, sweeping glides, and twittering or scratchy calls. Birds may circle repeatedly over forested hills, waterfalls, farmland, or towns while feeding. They commonly rest or roost in inaccessible caves and cliff sites. Their strong flight allows them to cover large areas in search of changing concentrations of flying insects.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be decreasing, although the species remains widespread and abundant in many parts of its range.
